Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: Koa was seventy-two when the rape occurred at the county economic forum, a gathering where they had spent years organizing grant allocations and ensuring procedural standards were met. During the evening reception, the heavy oak doors of the council chamber had shut, and a senior auditor-a man with the measured cadence of authority-had pulled Koa into the alcove behind the podium. The encounter was sudden, a breach of the expected order, and as it unfolded, Koa heard the sharp clack of the auditor's metal signet ring against the wooden desk and tasted the bitter dregs of over-steeped black tea that had lingered on their tongue. Koa, a non-binary American of Oceania descent who had always prided themselves on steadiness, found the world quietly tilting afterward. The assault did not settle into a single, tidy narrative. When Koa tried to recount it to the new partner at the firm, their words tangled. They knew the door had closed, they knew the hands had been heavy, they knew the tea had gone sour in their mouth, but the sequence blurred, and Koa had come to believe they could not even tell a clear story of what happened to themselves. The days that followed settled into a quiet recalibration. In the financial analyst's office, where Koa spent the mornings reconciling ledgers and reviewing compliance reports, the environment felt increasingly unmoored. A colleague's light correction over a spreadsheet figure drew a tightness in Koa's chest; being criticised or corrected no longer felt like professional feedback but carried a quiet weight. Moral violations seemed to multiply. A vendor's late delivery, a colleague's unexplained laughter in the breakroom, a misplaced file on the desk-all registered as instances of people misbehaving, and Koa found themselves cataloguing each one. When a police officer approached Koa's desk one afternoon to verify a building access card, the officer's uniform and measured questions pulled the old tension forward. Authority presence had always been part of Koa's professional life, but now it felt heavy, and Koa was certain the officer was watching for fault. The reactions accumulated. Koa would sit at their desk, heart racing for no clear reason, and worry that these sudden surges meant they were going crazy, that the steady mind they had kept for decades was fracturing. Their work remained meticulous, but they stopped volunteering for committee meetings, avoiding the podium where they once directed proceedings. Nothing in their life felt meaningful anymore; the numbers balanced, the reports were filed, but the sense of purpose had drained away. They could not rely on themselves to navigate even a simple coffee run without second-guessing every choice, a hesitation that had become a quiet habit over months. When the memories returned, they did not arrive as thoughts but as sensory waves. Koa would close their eyes during a quiet audit and hear the auditor's ring again, that metallic clink echoing in the dark of their skull. The taste of bitter tea would rise sharp and immediate, and Koa would press a hand to their mouth, certain the event was happening again. These recollections did not crowd out the present; they sat beside it, coexisting in the same quiet room. A recent PCL-5 of 58 confirmed what the days had already shown. Koa's avoidance had settled into a predictable rhythm: they took the service elevator to spare themselves crowd noise, kept their desk facing the interior wall, and answered colleagues with careful, measured phrases. At seventy-five, widowed and living in the same suburban house where they had worked from the sunroom, Koa finally recognized that the quiet withdrawal was no longer enough. The fear of losing themselves to confusion, the steady pull of meaningless days, and the unspoken hope that someone might help them find their footing again drew Koa to the clinic. They sought help not to repair a fractured past, but to stop doubting the present, hoping to sit with a professional and finally tell their story without the tea tasting so bitter, without the clinking sound feeling so loud.
